fixes.old: The Marshall Court refused Marbury's commission by ruling that the section of the Judiciary Act of 1789 giving the Court that power was unconstitutional, establishing the Supreme Court's power of judicial review over acts of Congress.
fixes.new: The Marshall Court held that Marbury was legally entitled to his commission, but that it could not order its delivery: the section of the Judiciary Act of 1789 that gave the Court original jurisdiction to issue such writs of mandamus conflicted with Article III and was unconstitutional. This established the Supreme Court's power of judicial review over acts of Congress.
fixes.why: Misstates the disposition: the Court did not deny Marbury's right to the commission, it denied itself jurisdiction to compel delivery.

fixes.old: A Boston woman who held religious meetings in her home and taught that believers could receive grace directly from God without clergy mediation (antinomianism). Tried and banished in 1638, she challenged both Puritan orthodoxy and women's prescribed role.
fixes.new: A Boston woman who held religious meetings in her home and taught that believers could receive grace directly from God without clergy mediation (antinomianism). Tried and sentenced to banishment in 1637 and expelled in 1638, she challenged both Puritan orthodoxy and women's prescribed role.
fixes.why: Hutchinson's trial and sentence were November 1637; only her departure and excommunication fall in 1638.

fixes.old: A Puritan minister banished from Massachusetts in 1636 for arguing that church and state must be separated and that the king could not grant land already owned by Native peoples. He founded Providence, Rhode Island, with religious liberty and purchased Native land.
fixes.new: A Puritan minister banished from Massachusetts in 1635 for arguing that church and state must be separated and that the king could not grant land already owned by Native peoples. He founded Providence, Rhode Island, in 1636 with religious liberty and purchased Native land.
fixes.why: The General Court ordered Williams's banishment in October 1635; 1636 is the founding of Providence, not the banishment.

fixes.old: Largely nomadic or semi-nomadic groups (Ute, Apache, Sioux) who followed buffalo herds and gathered wild plants. Dry, sparse grassland could not support large permanent farming villages, so they lived in small, mobile bands.
fixes.new: Largely nomadic or semi-nomadic groups (Ute, Shoshone, Apache, Blackfoot) who hunted bison on foot and gathered wild plants. Dry, sparse grassland could not support large permanent farming villages, so they lived in small, mobile bands.
fixes.why: Before contact the Sioux were woodland people in Minnesota, not Plains buffalo nomads; mounted Plains culture postdates the horse (see card a666d50191).

fixes.old: The Union Pacific building west and the Central Pacific building east met at Promontory Point, Utah, in 1869. Federal land grants and loans funded it, and the labor came largely from Chinese immigrants in the West and Irish immigrants and veterans in the East.
fixes.new: The Union Pacific building west and the Central Pacific building east met at Promontory Summit, Utah, in 1869. Federal land grants and loans funded it, and the labor came largely from Chinese immigrants in the West and Irish immigrants and veterans in the East.
fixes.why: The 1869 golden spike was driven at Promontory Summit; Promontory Point is a different location on the Great Salt Lake.
